claim: When a surface's small imperfections (bumps, dents) are hard to judge under standard studio-lighting shading, switching the viewport MatCap to a high-contrast option (e.g. a busy/high-frequency matcap, a vertical-line matcap, or a plain red/single-tone matcap for gauging overall smoothness) makes them visible; the default studio matcap can hide the same bumps entirely.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript (6:53-7:44): narrator notes the object surface is 'reflecting' under studio lighting and switches Viewport Shading's matcap selector; states 'these matcaps allow us to see surface imperfections better,' demonstrates that bumps added to the surface are 'not so easy to tell' back on studio lighting, and that certain high-contrast matcaps and a vertical-line matcap 'allow us to quickly identify bumps in the surface,' while a plain red or single-tone matcap is preferred 'when I work with very smooth surfaces' to judge overall smoothness.
rejected_alternative: Judging surface quality only under the default studio-lighting matcap/material preview, where per the narration small bumps are 'not so easy to tell.'

claim: Cavity shading has two independently-tunable components with different diagnostic uses: Screen Cavity produces a thin, sharp bright/dark line exactly at sharp edges and corners (good for judging edge crispness), while World Cavity produces a soft, wide ambient-occlusion-like darkening in crevices (good for judging overall shape depth/volume); both can be enabled together with separate strength values.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript (7:44-8:45): narrator enables Cavity in Viewport Shading, distinguishes 'World Cavity, which basically adds some kind of ambient occlusion effect' from 'Screen Cavity... this adds this very bright edge to the sharp edges and this dark edge to all the corners,' summarized as 'Screen is very sharp and thin and World is soft and wider,' with separate strength/size/distance controls and a 'both' type option.
rejected_alternative: Relying on flat solid shading with no cavity, which per the narration made a detailed face read as if it were 'a nice big face' from a distance -- 'we can't really see all this details' from above.

claim: Enabling Random under Viewport Shading's color options assigns each separate object a distinct random flat color, which is a fast way to tell whether two visually touching or overlapping shapes are actually one object or two separate objects, without selecting anything.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript (8:45-9:10): narrator says it 'can be sometimes hard to distinguish which object is separated from each other,' enables Random under Viewport Shading > color, and demonstrates that 'without selecting this, we can see that these two cylindrical shapes belong to the same object' because they share one random color.
rejected_alternative: Clicking each shape individually to check its outliner/selection highlight in order to determine object boundaries.

claim: To work on one part of a scene/object in isolation, select it and press '/' (Numpad) to enter Local View rather than hiding everything else with H (or Shift+Ctrl+I to invert selection, then H); Local View shows only the selected elements without changing any object's hidden/visible state, so nothing needs to be manually re-hidden afterward, and pressing '/' again (or selecting a subset inside Local View and pressing M) restores or narrows the view without disturbing prior hide state.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript (12:54-14:27): narrator notes the H-to-hide / Ctrl+I-invert-then-H workaround has a downside -- 'sometimes you have objects hidden and you don't want to unhide them... when you do this, you always unhide all objects... even when working with the eyes, this can be quite time consuming' -- then introduces Local View ('/' on Numpad) as 'a better way to deal with that,' stating 'nothing is hidden over here, but we can only see these objects since we are now in local view,' with '/' again or selecting-and-pressing-M to leave/narrow it.
rejected_alternative: Select-and-hide (H) combined with Ctrl+I invert-selection-then-H, followed by Alt+H to restore -- explicitly called out in the transcript as unhiding every previously-hidden object indiscriminately, not just the ones hidden for this isolation step.
reason: Isolating one part of a build (e.g. a handle or spout being test-fit against a body) without disturbing an existing, deliberate hide state elsewhere in the scene is a real recurring need for this project's incremental part-by-part construction workflow, and the transcript gives a concrete reason to prefer Local View over the hide/invert/unhide-all pattern rather than treating them as interchangeable.

claim: Selecting a face in edit mode and pressing Shift+Numpad7 aligns the viewport camera to look straight down that face's normal; because the view is then perfectly perpendicular to the intended surface, any deviation in the surrounding geometry (a face that should be flush/flat but isn't) becomes visually apparent as an off-axis silhouette.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript (14:27-15:17): narrator selects a face in edit mode, hits Shift+Numpad7, states 'the view will be aligned to the normal of this selected face,' and then uses that dead-on view to observe 'this USB flash drive is not perfectly straight, same for this thing over here. So we could adjust this' -- i.e. the aligned view itself is the detection method for the modeling error.
rejected_alternative: Judging a face's flatness/alignment from an arbitrary orbit angle, where an off-axis deviation is harder to see because the view isn't perpendicular to the surface being checked.

claim: Pressing Alt+B and dragging a rectangular region temporarily clips the 3D viewport's visible geometry to that region only (view-only, not a Boolean or destructive cut), which lets you see and edit inside an otherwise fully enclosed shape; pressing Alt+B again removes the clip and restores full geometry.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript (15:17-15:53): narrator wants to 'work inside of this robot head... the whole object is in the way,' presses Alt+B, selects a visible region, notes 'the rest will be cutoff, but just for the view, not like Boolean or anything like that,' edits inside, then presses Alt+B again to remove the clipping border.
rejected_alternative: Zooming the camera literally inside the enclosed shape to try to see/edit its interior -- described in the transcript as the first thing tried ('we could try to zoom in here and then get inside') before switching to the clipping-region approach.

claim: Ctrl+Alt+Q splits the 3D viewport into four simultaneous views (a free/perspective view plus top, front, and right); the sidebar's View > Quad View panel exposes three independent toggles -- Lock (locked views default to orthographic top/front/right and can't be reoriented; unlocking lets each pane be freely rotated, even into its own perspective view), Box (dragging an object in one pane live-updates its position in all other panes), and Clip (adds a per-view clipping plane so geometry crossing a boundary line is cut from that view, useful in edit mode combined with X-Ray for seeing/editing hidden backside geometry from a fixed angle).
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript (15:53-17:41): narrator enables Quad View (Ctrl+Alt+Q or View > Area > Toggle Quad View), describes the four resulting panes, and walks through the sidebar's Quad View panel: disabling Lock allows 'completely free to change the perspective in each of those windows, You can even change to perspective view'; Box makes moving an object in one pane update 'all the other views... automatically'; Clip 'adds a kind of clip region... when I cross this line, this will be cut away, and this will also affect the other views,' demonstrated combined with X-Ray to 'see inside here directly and change anything here on the backside of the robot.'
rejected_alternative: Repeatedly orbiting a single 3D viewport between top/front/side/perspective angles to cross-check a build, losing the simultaneous side-by-side comparison that Quad View provides.
